concepts.title: useState
concepts.description: useState gives a function component its own persistent value and a setter to update it, but the setter's deferred, closure-based behavior causes two common bugs: lost updates from repeated same-render calls, and stale values read inside delayed callbacks.
learningObjectives: Describe what useState returns and what calling its setter actually does.
Use a functional update (setCount(c => c + 1)) and explain why it behaves differently from setCount(count + 1) when called multiple times in quick succession.
Explain the stale-closure bug in terms of the JS closure mechanism already covered in the JavaScript Foundations module.
Predict the value logged by a delayed callback (e.g. inside setTimeout) that reads state directly, given a sequence of state updates.
Choose between a functional update and a ref-based approach depending on whether new state needs to be computed or the latest value simply needs to be read.

sections.heading: useState Mechanics: The [value, setter] Pair
sections.body:
`const [state, setState] = useState(initialValue)` returns a two-element array, destructured into the current value and a setter function permanently bound to that particular piece of state for this component instance. `initialValue` is only used on the first render for this instance; on every later render, `useState` returns whatever was most recently set. If computing the initial value is expensive, pass a function (`useState(() => loadFromStorage())`): React calls it once, on the first render, instead of evaluating the expression on every render and discarding the result.

Calling `setState(newValue)` does two distinct things: it records `newValue` as the value React should use for this state the next time this component renders, and it schedules a re-render of the component. The two always go together: you can't schedule a re-render without providing the new value, or store a value without React noticing. Note the phrase *the next time this component renders*: calling the setter does not change the `state` variable in the render that's currently executing. That variable is a constant for the duration of this render, fixed when `useState` returned it.

sections.heading: Functional Updates: setCount(c => c + 1)
The Stale Closure Bug: Reading State in a Delayed Callback
sections.body:
This is the JS closure mechanism from the JavaScript Foundations module, showing up as a common React bug. Every render creates new function values for everything defined in the component body: event handlers and, importantly, callbacks passed to `setTimeout`, `setInterval` or `.then()`. Each of those functions closes over the state values as they were *during that render*. Because `count` is a `const` created fresh by each call of the component, the `count` a callback sees is the one from the render where the callback was created, and it never changes afterward.

If a component schedules a `setTimeout` whose callback reads a state variable *directly* (not through a functional update), the callback keeps the value that state had in the render where the timeout was scheduled, however many renders and newer values occur before it fires. The callback isn't 'watching' the state; it closed over one value when it was created.

sections.heading: A Stale-Closure Timeline
Fixing Stale Closures: Functional Updates and Their Limits

examples.title: Same-Render Increments: Plain Value vs Functional Update
examples.explanation: In DoubleIncrementBroken, both setCount(count + 1) calls close over the same count from this render (say 0), so both mean 'set state to 1', and applying that twice still leaves 1. In DoubleIncrementFixed, each functional update receives the latest pending value: the first turns 0 into 1, and the second, because React processes queued updates to the same state in order, receives that 1 and turns it into 2. Only the functional form chains off the previous update instead of a shared render-time snapshot.

examples.title: A Stale Closure Inside setTimeout
examples.explanation: When "Log in 2s" is clicked, the handleLogLater created during the current render schedules a timeout callback that closes over that render's count. Later "+1" clicks produce new renders with their own increment and handleLogLater functions and their own count values, but they can't reach back and update a callback that's already scheduled. Two seconds later the callback logs the count from the render where it was created, which can be several increments behind what the screen shows.

misconceptions.description: Calling the setter updates the state variable immediately, so I can read the new value on the very next line of the same function.
misconceptions.clarification: Calling setState schedules an update and a re-render; it does not change the `state` variable currently in scope, which is a constant for the duration of this render. Reading `state` on the line after `setState(newValue)`, in the same function call, still gives the OLD value. The new value exists only when the component function runs again, on the next render.
misconceptions.fact: Calling setState schedules an update and a re-render; it does not reach back and mutate the `state` variable currently in scope, which is a plain constant for the duration of this render.

misconceptions.description: Calling setCount(count + 1) twice in a row should always increment by 2, since the setter was called twice.
misconceptions.clarification: Both calls, within one function call, close over the same count from that render, so both mean 'set state to count + 1', applied twice, for a single increment. Only functional updates (setCount(c => c + 1)) chain off each other's result, because each is evaluated against the most recently queued value instead of a shared render-time snapshot.

exercises.prompt: A user clicks "+1" once (count becomes 1). They then click "Log in 2s" (scheduling the timeout below). Within the next second, before the timeout fires, they click "+1" two more times (count becomes 3). What does the console log two seconds after "Log in 2s" was clicked, and why?
hints: handleLogLater is a function created during a specific render. Which render's count did the setTimeout callback close over: the one when the timeout was scheduled, or whatever count is when it fires?

Clicking +1 after scheduling the timeout triggers new renders, each with its own new increment function and its own count. Does creating those new functions modify the timeout callback that's already scheduled?
Each render has its own `count` constant, and a callback only ever sees the one from the render where it was created. Which render was that?
exercises.expectedAnswer: "count is 1" is logged, not 3. The setTimeout callback closed over the count (1) from the render active when "Log in 2s" was clicked. The two later "+1" clicks create new function instances closing over newer counts (2, then 3), which don't affect the callback already scheduled.
exercises.solutionExplanation: By the time "Log in 2s" is clicked, the earlier "+1" click has caused a re-render, so count is 1 in that render, and handleLogLater's setTimeout callback closes over that value: 1. The closure was formed when the function was created, over what was in scope then; it doesn't track count going forward. The next two "+1" clicks each cause a render that creates a new increment function and a new (never-scheduled) handleLogLater closing over 2 and then 3. The ORIGINAL timeout callback, already waiting since the earlier click, is a separate function instance and is unaffected. Two seconds after "Log in 2s", it runs and logs the only count it ever had, 1, even though the component's current count is by then 3.

exercises.prompt: Clicking "+3" is supposed to increase the count by 3, but it only ever increases it by 1 per click. Find the bug and fix it.
hints: All three setCount(count + 1) calls in the loop happen during the same call to addThree. Which value of count does each one close over?
Are these three calls 'add one on top of whatever the last call produced', or three copies of the same instruction?
What kind of update lets each call build on the previous one's result, instead of all reading the same render-time value?
exercises.solutionExplanation: All three loop iterations run within the same call to addThree, so all three setCount(count + 1) calls close over the same count from this render (say 0). Each is 'set state to 1', repeated three times, for a single increment. The functional form, setCount((c) => c + 1), fixes it because React applies queued functional updates to the same state in order, each operating on the result of the one before: the first turns 0 into 1, the second turns that 1 into 2, the third turns that 2 into 3, for +3 per click.

options: 3, because setCount was called three times, each adding one.
0, because calling setCount with a plain value never actually updates state.
1, because all three calls close over the same render's count value (0), so each one independently evaluates to 'set state to 1.'
It depends on network latency, since setCount is an asynchronous network call.
assessments.explanation: All three calls happen within the same execution of handleClick, so all three read the count captured in this render's closure, 0. Each evaluates count + 1 using that 0 and produces 1; React doesn't chain them into a running total, so the result is 1, not 3. The “3, because setCount was called three times…” option assumes each call builds on the previous call's result, which plain-value setState calls don't do (functional updates do). The “0, because calling setCount with a plain…” option is false: setCount(count + 1) does update state, just not additively. The “It depends on network latency, since setCount…” option is wrong: setCount is a synchronous scheduling call, not a network request.

assessments.prompt: Explain, in terms of how JavaScript closures work, why a setTimeout callback defined inside a component can end up logging an outdated value of a state variable, even though the component's displayed output is fully up to date.
assessments.modelAnswer: Every render of a component is a fresh call to the component's function, and any function defined inside that call, including a callback passed to setTimeout, is a new function value created on that render. Like any JavaScript closure, the callback's access to the surrounding scope is fixed by where it was written and what was in scope when it was created. So if the callback reads a state variable directly (say, `count`), it reads the value that variable held during the render where the callback was defined: a snapshot, not a live link to 'whatever count currently is.' If the component re-renders several times between scheduling and firing, each re-render produces its own state values and its own new (never-scheduled) versions of the callback, and none of that modifies the callback instance already waiting in the timer queue. It keeps the value it closed over. Meanwhile the component's JSX is recalculated on every render from the current state, so the screen stays up to date; only the old callback's closure is stale. This is related to, but not the same as, the classic var-in-a-loop bug: there, all callbacks share one variable that has since changed, while here each render has its own constant `count` and the callback simply keeps seeing the old one.

assessments.prompt: A developer wants a setTimeout callback to log the truly latest count, several seconds later, without setting any new state. They consider wrapping the read in a functional update, like `setCount(c => { console.log("count is", c); return c; })`, hoping that fixes the staleness the same way it fixes the double-increment bug. Does this actually solve the read-only staleness problem, and why?
options: Not really the intended tool for this -- a functional update's callback only runs internally, as part of applying a state update; it's designed to compute a new value to store, not to hand a live, always-current value to arbitrary code (like a console.log) at a point where nothing is actually being set. A ref kept in sync with the state is the standard tool for that read-only case instead.
No -- functional updates only work when called synchronously, in the same tick as the state was declared, so they can never be used inside a setTimeout at all.
No -- useState only accepts one functional update per component for its entire lifetime, so this would throw on the second call.
Yes -- functional updates always give you the live, current value no matter where or how they're used, so this pattern is a universal fix for stale closures of any kind.
assessments.explanation: Functional updates fix staleness when a callback computes a new state value from the latest queued value; that's why setCount(c => c + 1) chains correctly. Reading the latest value only to log or compare it is a different problem. Calling setCount just to run console.log inside the updater misuses the setter: it may schedule a re-render, the updater isn't guaranteed to run at that moment (React may defer it to the next render), and updaters should be pure (in Strict Mode development React calls them twice, so the log would appear twice). The standard tool for 'I just need the latest value, read-only, inside a stale callback' is a ref kept in sync with the state, since a ref's .current is read at call time through the same persistent object instead of a value captured when the closure was created.

concepts.title: useEffect
concepts.description: useEffect lets a component synchronize with something outside React's rendering (a subscription, a fetch, a timer), running after render completes, guided by a dependency array that must list every reactive value the effect reads, and cleaned up via an optional returned function before the next run and on unmount.
learningObjectives: Explain what an effect is for, and why it runs after render rather than during it.
Explain why omitting a dependency an effect reads is a correctness bug, not just a missed optimization.
Write and explain the purpose of a cleanup function returned from an effect.
Diagnose why a given effect causes an infinite render loop and fix it.
Distinguish situations that need an effect from ones that are better handled as a plain calculation during render.

sections.heading: What Effects Are For: Synchronizing With the Outside World
sections.body:
A component takes props and state and produces a description of UI, and that calculation is supposed to be pure: the same inputs give the same output, with no side effects. But real applications need to reach *outside* that model: subscribing to a WebSocket or a browser event, touching a DOM node beyond what JSX expresses, calling an external API, starting a timer, writing to localStorage. Each of these is a **side effect**, and `useEffect` is the hook for saying 'after this component renders (or re-renders), synchronize with X.'

The timing matters: an effect runs **after** render, once React has updated the real DOM to match that render's output, never during the render calculation. That keeps rendering a predictable, side-effect-free calculation of 'what should the UI look like', with anything that reaches outside pushed into a separate phase afterward.

sections.heading: The Dependency Array
The Cleanup Function
The Classic Infinite-Loop Bug
A Complete Data-Fetching Effect

examples.title: Subscribing to window resize, with cleanup
examples.explanation: The empty dependency array means this effect runs once after the first render (in development Strict Mode it runs, cleans up and runs again), subscribing to the resize event. The dependencies never change, so the cleanup only runs when WindowWidth unmounts, but it would matter just as much if the effect re-ran: without it each run would add another resize listener without removing the previous one, and a single resize would call setWidth once per leftover listener.

examples.title: The Infinite Loop, and the Fix
examples.explanation: BuggyCounter's effect is triggered by count changing, and it changes count every time it runs: render, effect, count changes, re-render, effect again, forever. FixedCounter only reacts to an external signal (resetSignal) unrelated to the count it sets, which breaks the cycle: changing count doesn't change resetSignal, so the effect doesn't re-trigger itself. An effect that both depends on and unconditionally overwrites the same state usually means a guard condition is missing, or that the logic would be simpler as a plain calculation during render.

misconceptions.description: useEffect runs during render, so it's fine to use it to compute a value this render's JSX needs.
misconceptions.clarification: Effects run AFTER the DOM has been updated to match a completed render -- never during the render calculation itself. Anything the current render's JSX needs should be computed in the component body (or via useMemo), not produced in an effect and stored in a separate state variable: effect-plus-setState adds an extra render of lag for something that could be a synchronous calculation with no extra state.
misconceptions.fact: Effects run AFTER the DOM has already been updated to match a completed render -- never during the render calculation itself.

misconceptions.description: The dependency array is mainly about performance -- leaving something out just means the effect re-runs a bit more or less than ideal, but it still works correctly either way.
misconceptions.clarification: Omitting a dependency the effect reads is a correctness bug, not a performance tradeoff. The effect function is a closure formed on the render that last caused it to run; if a value it reads isn't listed, nothing re-runs the effect when that value changes, so it keeps using the old value from its last run, the same stale-closure mechanism covered for useState. Disabling the exhaustive-deps lint warning hides the symptom without fixing the bug.

exercises.prompt: This component is supposed to re-run its search whenever the query prop changes, but after mounting it never searches again, however many times query changes, and always shows results for the query from the first render. Find the bug and fix it.
hints: The dependency array is empty. What does that tell React about when this effect may run again?
The eslint-disable comment is suppressing a real warning. What is the linter telling you about the values this effect body reads?
The effect body reads `query`. If query isn't in the dependency array, does the effect ever get a reason to notice that it changed?
exercises.solutionExplanation: An empty dependency array means 'run after the first render and not again', so this effect fetches once, with the query from the first render, and never runs again however often the query prop changes. The eslint-disable comment suppressed the warning that would have caught this: the effect reads query but doesn't list it, so it stays closed over query's first value. The fix lists query in the dependency array (and removes the eslint-disable comment), so the effect re-runs and re-fetches whenever query changes. A production version would also add an `isCurrent` guard like the earlier example, so a slow response for an old query can't overwrite a newer one.

exercises.prompt: This component is meant to keep a copy of the current preferences in localStorage, but as soon as it mounts it re-renders continuously and the tab becomes unresponsive. Find the bug and fix it.
hints: The effect depends on prefs, and it calls setPrefs with a new object built via {...prefs, ...} on every run. Is that object ever considered 'unchanged', even if lastSavedFor already equals userId?
The dependency comparison checks whether the reference changed, not whether the content did. What does a fresh object built with the spread operator look like from that perspective?
Does writing to localStorage require calling setPrefs at all?
exercises.solutionExplanation: Every run of this effect calls setPrefs({ ...prefs, lastSavedFor: userId }), which builds a new object with the spread operator: a new reference every time, whether or not any field's value changed. The dependency array is [prefs], so after every run React sees a changed dependency, re-renders and runs the effect again, which produces another new object, forever. It's the same loop as an effect depending on state it unconditionally rewrites, with an object reference making the 'changed every time' less obvious. Persisting prefs to localStorage never needed setPrefs; removing that call leaves an effect that mirrors real changes in prefs to localStorage, with nothing to trigger itself.

assessments.prompt: A teammate says: "I left `userId` out of this effect's dependency array on purpose, since I only want it to run once, and it's a minor performance tweak either way." The effect reads `userId` inside its body. What's the accurate assessment?
options: That's incorrect -- effects with any dependency array shorter than the number of props the component receives will throw a runtime error.
That's incorrect -- omitting a dependency the effect actually reads means the effect's closure keeps using the userId value from whichever render it last ran on.
That's correct -- dependency arrays are purely a performance optimization, so leaving one out just means the effect might run slightly more or less often than ideal.
That's correct, but only because useEffect automatically reruns for every prop change regardless of what's listed in the dependency array.
assessments.explanation: The dependency array tells React when to re-run an effect by comparing each listed value to its value on the previous render; it says nothing about values NOT listed. If the effect body reads userId but userId isn't listed, nothing triggers the effect when userId changes, so it keeps using the userId from the render where it last ran: a correctness bug (stale data), not a missed optimization. The “That's incorrect -- effects with any dependency…” option describes a rule that doesn't exist; there is no such runtime check. The “That's correct, but only because useEffect automatically…” option is false: useEffect only reacts to what's listed in its dependency array; it doesn't track every prop.

assessments.prompt: While reviewing a pull request, you see a useEffect call with `// eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` directly above it, added to silence a warning about a missing dependency. What would you say in the code review, and what would you ask the author to do instead?
assessments.modelAnswer: I'd flag this before merging rather than let it be suppressed, because the exhaustive-deps warning is almost always catching a real bug: the effect closes over a reactive value it reads, and if that value isn't a dependency, the effect won't notice when it changes and keeps operating on stale data from the render where it last ran, the same stale-closure mechanism as with useState. Disabling the rule removes the signal that the bug exists, which makes it harder to find later, when the symptom (a stale value showing up downstream) is separated from the cause by more code and time. I'd ask the author to add the missing dependency and confirm the effect still behaves when it re-runs on that value's changes (adding a cleanup if the effect does something that must be undone between runs, like a subscription or timer). If there's a good reason the value shouldn't be a dependency (it's a ref, or it's meant to be read only on mount, or it should be wrapped with useEffectEvent), the code should say so in a comment explaining why, instead of a bare eslint-disable. The rule is occasionally overzealous, but that's a reason to understand why it fires in this case, not to silence it when it's inconvenient.

options: Both intervals keep running side by side indefinitely, since useEffect never automatically cleans up a timer.
The new interval (ticking "B") starts first, and the old interval (ticking "A") is cleared afterward, so both briefly run at the same time.
Nothing happens until the component unmounts entirely -- the cleanup function only ever runs then, never in response to label changing.
The old interval (ticking "A") is cleared first, and only then does a brand-new interval (ticking "B") start.
assessments.explanation: The returned cleanup function runs right before the effect runs again for new dependency values, not only on unmount. When label changes to "B", React first calls the cleanup from the PREVIOUS run (clearInterval(id) for the "A" interval) and then runs the effect body again, creating a new interval that ticks "B". That ordering means two intervals never overlap, which is the duplication problem cleanup exists to prevent. The “Nothing happens until the component unmounts entirely…” option describes only half of when cleanup runs -- it also runs on unmount, but that's not the only trigger.

concepts.title: useRef
concepts.description: useRef gives a component a mutable value that persists across renders and doesn't trigger a re-render when it changes, which makes it the right tool for DOM node access and for internal bookkeeping that shouldn't drive what's on screen.
learningObjectives: Explain what useRef returns and why the same object persists across every render of a component instance.
State the core contrast between changing state and changing a ref, in terms of what does and doesn't trigger a re-render.
Use a ref to call an imperative DOM method like .focus() on a real DOM node.
Use a ref to store an 'instance variable' style value, like a previous render's value or a timer id.
Decide, for a given value, whether it belongs in state or in a ref.

sections.heading: What useRef Gives You: A Mutable Box That Persists
sections.body: `useRef(initialValue)` returns a plain object shaped like `{ current: initialValue }`. What matters is that it's the *same object* on every render of a component instance: React creates it on the first render and hands back that identical object afterward. Writing `myRef.current = newValue` mutates that persistent box in place, and reading `myRef.current` later, even from a callback defined on an earlier render, returns whatever was most recently written. So there's no stale-closure problem as with state read in a delayed callback: you always read through the one live object, not a variable snapshotted into a particular render's closure.

sections.heading: State Change Re-renders, Ref Change Doesn't
sections.body:
The key fact about refs:

- Changing state (by calling its setter) tells React something changed: it schedules a re-render, the component function runs again, and the JSX reflects the new value.
- Changing a ref (`myRef.current = x`) tells React nothing. No re-render is scheduled, and unless something else causes one, the UI never reflects the change, however many times `.current` is reassigned.

So use a ref when the component needs to track or mutate a value, but a change to it should *not* by itself update anything on screen. If a change should be visible in the rendered output, it belongs in state; hiding it in a ref lets the UI drift out of sync with the data, the same problem as mutating state directly instead of going through its setter.

sections.heading: Accessing a DOM Node
Storing 'Instance Variable' Values
sections.body: Beyond DOM nodes, refs are the natural home for values a component remembers or mutates internally but that don't drive what's rendered: the previous value of some prop or state (to compare 'rising or falling'), an interval or timeout id (so a later handler or cleanup can clear it), a flag like 'has the initial fetch already happened', or a render counter used for debugging. Changing these shouldn't re-render the component; they're bookkeeping, not data the UI shows. Using state would work, but each change would trigger a re-render for a value nothing in the JSX reads. One rule: write to `ref.current` in event handlers and effects, not during rendering. Render should stay a pure calculation, and the React docs advise against reading or writing refs during render except for one-time initialization.

examples.title: Focusing an Input on Mount
examples.explanation: inputRef starts as null; React sets inputRef.current to the <input> DOM node once it exists, right after the first render commits. The effect (which runs after that commit, once, because of the empty dependency array) calls the DOM .focus() method on that node. No JSX prop expresses that declaratively, since 'focus yourself once, now' is a one-off command, not a piece of UI state to describe.

examples.title: Tracking a Previous Value Without Triggering Extra Renders
examples.explanation: prevCelsiusRef.current holds celsius as of the last effect run. The direction calculation runs during render, before this render's effect has updated the ref, so it compares the new celsius prop against the ref's value from BEFORE this render: the 'previous value' comparison. Writing to prevCelsiusRef.current doesn't trigger a re-render, and doesn't need to, since the celsius change already caused this render. Treat this as a demonstration of the mechanics rather than a pattern to copy: it reads a ref during render, and any re-render not caused by celsius changing (a parent re-render, say) sees the updated ref and shows 'steady'. When the previous value drives what's displayed, the React docs suggest keeping it in state instead.

misconceptions.description: Changing a ref's .current value should update what's on screen, the same way calling a state setter does, since it's still 'data belonging to the component.'
misconceptions.clarification: Changing a ref never schedules a re-render, no matter what. State and ref changes send different signals to React: a state setter says 'something changed, please re-render'; a ref mutation says nothing. If a value's changes need to be visible in the UI, it has to be state (or derived from state); a ref holding the 'right' value doesn't help if nothing re-renders to display it.
misconceptions.fact: Changing a ref never schedules a re-render, no matter what.

misconceptions.description: Refs are basically a faster version of state -- I should prefer them for values that change often, to avoid extra re-renders.
misconceptions.clarification: This only makes sense if the UI never needs to reflect that value's changes. Using a ref just to dodge re-renders, for a value whose changes SHOULD show on screen, leaves the screen out of sync with the data, the same bug as mutating state directly. Refs aren't 'state, but cheaper'; they're for values that fall outside what the rendered output shows.

exercises.prompt: A user clicks "Click me" three times, then clicks "Force re-render" once. What does the "Displayed click count" text show immediately after each of the three "Click me" clicks, and what does it show after "Force re-render" is clicked?
hints: Does mutating clickCountRef.current, on its own, cause ClickTracker to run again and produce fresh JSX?
The JSX text only reflects clickCountRef.current at the moment the component renders. What causes a render here, and what doesn't?
When 'Force re-render' is clicked and setRenderCount triggers a new render, what value is in clickCountRef.current?
exercises.expectedAnswer: After each of the three 'Click me' clicks the text still shows 'Displayed click count: 0', even though clickCountRef.current is 1, then 2, then 3 (as the console logs show). Only after 'Force re-render' does the text update, jumping to 'Displayed click count: 3', the ref's value when that render happens.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Mutating clickCountRef.current in handleClick never schedules a re-render; React doesn't see ref changes. So ClickTracker doesn't re-run after any of the three 'Click me' clicks, and the JSX, evaluated only on the initial render when the ref was 0, keeps showing 0, even though the ref holds 1, then 2, then 3 (which the console.log lines show). 'Force re-render' calls setRenderCount, a state update, which does schedule a re-render; ClickTracker runs again, evaluates {clickCountRef.current} fresh, finds 3, and the text jumps from 0 to 3, skipping 1 and 2, which were never rendered.

assessments.prompt: Which of these changes, by itself, causes a component to re-render?
options: Mutating a ref's .current property.
Reading a prop's current value inside the component body.
Declaring a new local variable with let inside the component function.
Calling a state setter function returned by useState.
assessments.explanation: Calling a state setter is one of React's triggers for scheduling a re-render; it's the mechanism for saying 'something changed, please run this component again.' Mutating a ref's .current (“Mutating a ref's .current property”) is the opposite case: React can't know, and schedules nothing. Reading a prop (“Reading a prop's current value inside the component body”) changes nothing; a prop only changes because the parent re-rendered and passed something new. Declaring a local variable (“Declaring a new local variable with let…”) has no effect on React's rendering; it's ordinary JavaScript scoped to one function call.

options: handlePlayClick secretly runs inside an implicit useEffect, so React automatically delays calling it until videoRef.current is non-null.
React automatically calls .play() itself as soon as the ref attaches, making handlePlayClick's own call redundant but harmless.
The ref is set when React commits the first render, which happens before any click can occur.
useRef never actually returns null as its current value, no matter what argument is passed to useRef(...).
assessments.explanation: videoRef.current starts as null and becomes the DOM node once React has mounted the <video> element, which happens when the first render commits, before the user can interact with anything on the page. Since handlePlayClick only runs in response to a click on an already-rendered button, the <video> element (and videoRef.current) already exists by then. If the <video> were rendered conditionally, the ref could be null again after it unmounts, and a check would be needed. The “useRef never actually returns null…” option is false: useRef(null) does start as null, which is the point of passing null as the initial value; it's the timing of when the ref is later updated that makes a null check unnecessary here.

concepts.title: useMemo and useCallback
concepts.description: useMemo caches an expensive computed value and useCallback caches a function reference (it's useMemo specialized for functions). Both rely on JavaScript's referential-equality rules, and both are optimizations with a cost of their own, not something to apply everywhere by default.
learningObjectives: Explain referential equality and why two structurally identical objects, arrays, or functions are not === equal.
Explain why a function or object literal written inside a component body is a new value on every render.
Distinguish what useMemo memoizes from what useCallback memoizes, and explain why useCallback is really useMemo specialized for functions.
Identify the situations where memoization has a payoff versus where it's needless overhead.
Fix a bug caused by an unstable object or function reference being used as a dependency.

sections.heading: Referential Equality: Same Contents, Different Identity
sections.body:
JavaScript's `===` operator compares objects, arrays and functions by **identity** (are they the same value in memory?), not by comparing their contents field by field:

```javascript
console.log({ a: 1 } === { a: 1 });          // false
console.log([1, 2, 3] === [1, 2, 3]);        // false
console.log((() => {}) === (() => {}));       // false

const obj = { a: 1 };
console.log(obj === obj);                     // true -- same reference
```

Primitives (numbers, strings, booleans, null, undefined) differ: `===` compares them by value, so `5 === 5` and `"hi" === "hi"` are true. Two functions with identical bodies are still two distinct function objects if they come from two separate function expressions, and `===` says false whatever is inside them.

sections.heading: Every Render Creates New Objects, Arrays, and Functions
useMemo: Memoizing a Computed Value
sections.body:
```jsx
const result = useMemo(() => computeExpensiveValue(a, b), [a, b]);
```

`useMemo` runs the function you give it and caches the returned value. On later renders it re-runs the function only if a listed dependency changed since the previous render; otherwise it returns the same cached value, reference and all. There are two possible payoffs: skipping an expensive recomputation and, often more important in practice, keeping a stable reference across renders when the value is compared by identity downstream (as a dependency of another hook, or as a prop into a memoized child). Treat it as a performance hint, not a guarantee: React may discard cached values (for example while rebuilding the tree), so your code must still be correct if the function re-runs.

sections.heading: useCallback: useMemo for Functions
The Cost: Optimizations Aren't Free
sections.body:
Both hooks cost something on every render, whether or not they recompute: React checks each listed dependency and keeps the cached value and its dependency list in memory. For a cheap computation, or a function never compared by identity anywhere that matters, useMemo/useCallback adds overhead and code for no benefit. 'Memoize everything, just in case' is an anti-pattern, and it makes components harder to read.

Besides a genuinely slow calculation, they earn their keep in two reference-identity situations: (1) the memoized value or function is a *dependency of another hook* (like useEffect), which would otherwise see a 'new' dependency on every render and re-run for nothing; and (2) a function or object is passed as a prop to a child wrapped in `React.memo`, which would otherwise see a 'changed' prop every render (the reference is always new) and defeat the `React.memo`. Outside those, reach for useMemo/useCallback once you've measured a cost worth solving. Also note that the React Compiler (a build-time tool, stable since late 2025) can add this kind of memoization automatically in projects that use it, so hand-written memoization matters most where you don't use the compiler or need precise control over a dependency.

examples.title: Referential Equality, Demonstrated
examples.code:
console.log({ a: 1 } === { a: 1 });          // false: different objects
console.log([1, 2, 3] === [1, 2, 3]);        // false: different arrays
console.log((() => {}) === (() => {}));       // false: different functions

const obj = { a: 1 };
console.log(obj === obj);                     // true: the SAME reference

console.log(5 === 5);                         // true: primitives compare by value
console.log("hi" === "hi");                   // true
examples.explanation: Every === comparison between two separately created objects, arrays or functions returns false, however identical their contents look: === on these types checks whether both sides point to the same thing in memory. Only comparing a value to itself (one reference, stored and reused) returns true. Primitives compare by value, which is why 5 === 5 and "hi" === "hi" are true; a primitive has no identity apart from its value.

examples.title: useCallback Preserving a Stable Reference for React.memo
examples.explanation: React.memo makes ExpensiveList skip re-rendering when its props are all reference-equal to last time. Without useCallback, handleItemClick would be a new function on every render of Parent, so each click on the button would give ExpensiveList a 'new' onItemClick, even though the function does the same thing, and React.memo's shallow comparison would re-render ExpensiveList anyway. With useCallback and an empty dependency array, handleItemClick keeps the same reference across every render of Parent, so ExpensiveList sees an unchanged onItemClick and skips re-rendering when only count changes. (The empty array is safe here because the handler only uses `console.log`; a handler that read state or props would need them listed.)

misconceptions.description: Two objects (or arrays, or functions) with exactly the same contents should be === equal, since they represent 'the same data.'
misconceptions.clarification: === for objects, arrays, and functions compares identity (are these literally the same value in memory), not structural content. {a: 1} === {a: 1} is false, even though both sides look identical, because they're two separately created objects. Only comparing a value to itself (the same reference, stored once and reused) returns true. Primitives like numbers and strings compare by value.
misconceptions.fact: === for objects, arrays, and functions compares identity (are these literally the same value in memory), not structural content. {a: 1} === {a: 1} is false, even though both sides look identical, because they're two separately created objects.

misconceptions.description: Wrapping every function and computed value in useCallback/useMemo is always at least harmless, so it's safer to just do it everywhere.
misconceptions.clarification: Memoization has a cost every render (comparing dependencies, holding cached values and dependency lists in memory), and for a value never compared by reference downstream (not a hook dependency, not a prop into a React.memo'd child) that cost buys nothing. Using useMemo/useCallback everywhere 'just in case' adds overhead and reading complexity; they're targeted tools for identity problems, not a safety habit.

exercises.prompt: This effect is supposed to re-run the search only when query changes, but it fires on every render of SearchResults. Find both issues and fix them.
hints: options is an object literal written inside the component body. What's true about its reference on every render, whether or not its contents change?
The dependency array compares options by reference, not by contents. What does that comparison give when options is a new object every render?
Separately, the effect body also reads query. Is it listed where it needs to be?
exercises.solutionExplanation: There are two bugs. First, options is a fresh object literal on every render, a new reference each time even though {caseSensitive: false, limit: 10} never changes in content, so as a dependency it makes the effect fire on every render regardless of query. Wrapping it in useMemo with an empty dependency array gives it a stable reference (it changes only if its own deps change, here never). Since options doesn't depend on props or state, defining it at module level outside the component, or inside the effect, works equally well and avoids the hook. Second, the effect body reads query but the original dependency array never listed it, a stale-closure bug: once the first problem is fixed, the effect would keep searching with the query from its first run. The fixed version lists query and the memoized options, so the effect re-runs when query changes and not just because options was recreated.

assessments.prompt: A component computes `const total = items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);` from a small array of 5 items, on every render, and this value isn't passed to any other hook's dependency array or to a React.memo'd child. Should this be wrapped in useMemo?
options: No -- summing 5 items is cheap, and since the result isn't used anywhere that cares about referential identity or expensive recomputation, useMemo would add the cost of a dependency check and cached-value bookkeeping for no benefit.
Yes, but only because reduce() is always considered an expensive operation in React.
No -- useMemo cannot be used with array methods like reduce().
Yes, always -- any computed value should be memoized as a general best practice.
assessments.explanation: useMemo earns its cost when the computation is expensive, or when the value's reference identity matters downstream (as a dependency of another hook, or a prop into a React.memo'd child). Neither applies here: summing 5 numbers is trivial, and nothing downstream compares this value by reference. Wrapping it would mean paying for a dependency comparison and cached-value storage every render to skip a computation that was already almost free, a net loss. The “Yes, always -- any computed value should…” option is the 'memoize everything just in case' anti-pattern. The “Yes, but only because reduce() is always…” option is false: reduce() over a small array isn't expensive; cost depends on what's computed and over how much data. The “No -- useMemo cannot be used…” option is false: useMemo works with any computation, reduce() included.

options: This throws a runtime error immediately, since useCallback requires at least one dependency to be listed in its array.
handleSubmit is memoized once, on the first render, and its closure over query is frozen at that render's value (the empty string) forever.
handleSubmit automatically re-creates itself whenever query changes regardless of the dependency array, since useCallback always tracks every piece of state referenced in its function body.
Nothing -- an empty dependency array is always the correct choice for an event handler wrapped in useCallback.
assessments.explanation: useCallback(fn, deps) behaves like useMemo(() => fn, deps): it's useMemo specialized for functions, so the same dependency rules and stale-closure risk apply as for any memoized value or effect. handleSubmit reads query in its body but query isn't in the dependency array, so handleSubmit is created once (closing over query as it was on the first render, an empty string) and never recreated. Every later call still passes that original query to onSearch, whatever the user has typed. It's the same 'omitting a dependency you read is a correctness bug' rule from useEffect, showing up through useCallback. (The code also omits onSearch from the array; the linter would flag both.)

concepts.title: Custom Hooks
concepts.description: A custom hook is a regular function, named starting with 'use', that calls other hooks to bundle up reusable stateful logic. The Rules of Hooks exist because React matches hook calls to their stored state by call order on every render.
learningObjectives: Explain what makes a function a 'custom hook,' and why the useX naming convention matters practically.
State the Rules of Hooks and explain, in terms of call order, why breaking them causes state to attach to the wrong hook call.
Extract a repeated stateful pattern (like fetch-with-loading-and-error) into a reusable custom hook.
Identify a violation of the Rules of Hooks in given code and fix it.

sections.heading: A Custom Hook Is Just a Function
sections.body: There's no special React API for declaring a custom hook. It's an ordinary JavaScript function that calls one or more other hooks in its body and, by convention, is named starting with `use` (`useWindowWidth`, `useFetch`, `useDebounce`). The naming isn't cosmetic: it's how the linter (`eslint-plugin-react-hooks`) recognizes that the function follows the Rules of Hooks and may call other hooks, and it tells other developers what constraints apply when calling it. Naming it `getWindowWidth` instead of `useWindowWidth` breaks nothing in the language, but the linter can no longer check hook usage inside it, and the name misleads readers about what the function does internally and where it's safe to call.

sections.heading: Why Extract a Custom Hook
sections.body: The point is reuse. When several components need the same combination of hooks working together (subscribing to window resize and tracking the width; tracking online/offline status; fetching a URL and tracking loading/error state), pulling it into one named function avoids copy-pasting the same useState/useEffect/useRef calls everywhere. It also names the pattern, so each component that uses it is shorter and says *what* it does (`const { data, loading, error } = useFetch(url);`) rather than *how*.

sections.heading: The Rules of Hooks and Call Order
sections.body:
Two rules govern every hook, custom or built-in. First, only call hooks at the top level of a component (or another hook), never inside an `if`, a loop, a nested function, or after an early `return`. Second, only call hooks from function components or other custom hooks, never from ordinary JavaScript functions or class components.

The reason: React doesn't track a component's hook state *by name*; it tracks it *by the order hooks are called in*, on every render, for a component instance. Roughly, 'the 1st hook call this component makes is always this state slot; the 2nd is always that one', matched by position, render after render. If a hook call is skipped on some renders, every hook call *after* it shifts by one position relative to React's stored list. React hands back whatever it has stored at that position, which may belong to a different hook call than the one asking, so state and refs can get cross-wired to the wrong variable. If the *number* of hooks changes between renders, React usually notices and throws an error such as 'Rendered more hooks than during the previous render'; if the count stays the same but the order shifts (for example, two conditional branches each calling a different hook), the mismatch can go unreported. Either way, the code is wrong.

sections.heading: A Concrete Example: Extracting useFetch

examples.title: Extracting a Repeated Fetch Pattern Into useFetch
examples.explanation: UserProfile and ProductPage need the same 'fetch a URL, track loading and error' logic against different endpoints. Instead of duplicating three useState calls and a useEffect, both call the same useFetch hook. The hook calls run separately for each component instance (React tracks state per component instance, not per hook definition), so each component gets its own independent data/loading/error state from one shared implementation.

examples.title: Violating the Rules of Hooks
examples.explanation: When showDetails is true, this component calls useState twice, details then name. When it's false, it calls useState once: name. React tracks hook state by call order for this component instance, so when the first call is skipped, React's 'first hook slot' now refers to a different hook than before, and every call after it (here, name) reads or writes the wrong stored value. Because the number of hooks changes, React in practice usually throws ('Rendered more hooks than during the previous render' or 'Rendered fewer hooks than expected') when showDetails toggles; with an unchanged count the mismatch could be silent.

misconceptions.description: Custom hooks are a distinct React feature or API, separate from just writing an ordinary function.
misconceptions.clarification: There's no createHook function or API. A custom hook is a regular JavaScript function that calls other hooks, plus a naming convention (starting with use). The label describes how an ordinary function is used and named, not a separate mechanism React provides.

misconceptions.description: As long as a hook call definitely happens somewhere during a render, it doesn't matter whether it's inside an if statement or a loop -- the important thing is just that it eventually runs.
misconceptions.clarification: It matters, because React tracks hook state by call ORDER/position for a component instance across renders, not by name or by 'did it run at all this render.' If a hook call is present on some renders and absent on others, every hook call after it shifts position, and React matches stored state to the wrong hook call. Usually React throws an error such as 'Rendered more hooks than during the previous render'; when the count happens to match, the bug is silent and hard to diagnose.

exercises.prompt: Right after showDetails toggles, this component crashes with an error like 'Rendered more hooks than during the previous render' (and without that check, name and details would get each other's state). Find the Rules-of-Hooks violation and fix it.
hints: The useState call for details is inside an if block. Does that hook call happen on every render of Profile, or only on some?

React matches each useState call to its stored value by the ORDER hooks are called in during a render, not by variable name. What happens to that ordering across renders where showDetails is true versus false?

What would change if useState(null) for details were called unconditionally at the top, with the `if (showDetails)` check controlling only how the value is used or updated, not whether the hook is called?
exercises.solutionExplanation: Calling useState(null) for details only when showDetails is true means Profile sometimes calls useState twice per render (details, then name) and sometimes once (name). When the call count differs from the previous render, React's position-based matching of hook calls to stored state breaks: React throws a 'Rendered more/fewer hooks' error, and without that check name would read whatever sits in a different slot. The fix moves the useState(null) call for details to the top level so it runs on every render regardless of showDetails. The conditional logic (whether to fetch and populate it) stays inside the effect, where an if statement is fine, because useEffect itself is still called unconditionally and only the code *inside* it branches.

assessments.prompt: Why does calling a hook conditionally (e.g. inside an if statement) risk corrupting a component's state, rather than simply skipping that piece of state entirely on some renders?
options: Because React identifies each hook call by the variable name it's assigned to, and conditional calls confuse that name-matching process.
Because hooks can only be called a fixed maximum number of times per component, and a conditional call risks exceeding that limit.
Because React matches each hook call to its stored state purely by the order hooks are called in during a render.
Because conditionally calling a hook causes a JavaScript syntax error that only appears at runtime under specific conditions.
assessments.explanation: React has no name-based lookup for hooks (ruling out the “Because React identifies each hook call…” option); it relies on call order within a render, matched against the previous render's sequence of calls for that component instance. Skipping a hook call on some renders shifts the position of every hook call after it, so React hands back state (or a ref) intended for a different hook call, or throws a 'Rendered more/fewer hooks' error when the count differs. Either way the code parses and runs, which rules out the “Because conditionally calling a hook causes…” option. The “Because hooks can only be called…” option describes a limit that doesn't exist; the issue is consistent ordering across renders, not a call-count ceiling.

options: It also increases by 3, since both components are calling the same useCounter function and therefore share the same underlying count.
It resets back to 0, since a second component calling useCounter overwrites whatever state the first component's call had set up.
It becomes undefined, since a custom hook can only be safely called from a single component at a time.
It stays exactly at 100, completely unaffected -- each component instance that calls useCounter gets its own independent count state.
assessments.explanation: A custom hook is a regular function whose body calls other hooks, and React tracks the resulting state per component instance, not per function definition. CounterA and CounterB each call useCounter independently, and each call gets its own useState slot because they run in two different component instances. Sharing the useCounter implementation is like two components each calling useState directly: it bundles the pattern for reuse but creates no shared state. CounterB's count stays at its initial value of 100. To share state between components you'd lift it up or use context.

concepts.title: Context API
concepts.description: Context lets any descendant read a value without threading it through every intermediate component's props, but every consumer re-renders whenever the context's value changes, even if the field it reads didn't, so it's not a free substitute for well-scoped state.
learningObjectives: Explain the prop-drilling problem with an example of intermediate components forwarding a prop they don't use.
Use createContext, a Provider, and useContext to make a value available to a deeply nested descendant.
Explain why every consumer of a context re-renders when its value changes, even if the specific field that consumer reads is unaffected.
Judge whether a given piece of state is a good fit for context, or would cause more unnecessary re-rendering than it solves.

sections.heading: The Prop-Drilling Problem
createContext, Provider, and useContext
The Caveat: Every Consumer Re-renders on Value Change
Context Is Not a Free Global-State Replacement
sections.body: Because every consumer re-renders, putting a frequently changing value (mouse position, a per-keystroke input value, a message counter) into a context consumed across the tree can cause more unnecessary re-rendering than the prop drilling it replaced, especially when unrelated state is bundled into one context value, since changing any piece re-renders every consumer of the bundle. Context suits values that change rarely and are needed widely (theme, the authenticated user, locale settings, feature flags), not as a substitute for local state or ordinary props whenever passing something down feels tedious. When changes are frequent and consumption is broad, the usual first mitigation is to split one bundled context into several narrower ones, so a component subscribes only to what it needs, and to memoize each provider's value with `useMemo` so it changes only when its data does.

examples.title: Prop Drilling vs a Context Fix
examples.explanation: In the prop-drilling version, Sidebar and Panel accept and forward a theme prop only so ThemedButton can receive it. The context version removes theme from both signatures: ThemedButton reads from the nearest Provider above it via useContext, however many layers separate them, and Sidebar and Panel don't know theme exists.

examples.title: One Bundled Context Value Causing Unrelated Re-renders
examples.explanation: Clicking "Toggle theme" calls setTheme, which re-renders App and builds a new value object (a fresh object literal on every render of App). Because AppContext's value reference changed, both ThemeLabel and UserGreeting re-render (both console.log lines fire) even though user never changed. Both are wrapped in `memo` (imported from 'react'), so App's own re-render wouldn't re-render them; the context change does. UserGreeting only reads user, but useContext subscribes it to the whole value object, not the field it destructures.

misconceptions.description: Context replaces the need for prop drilling entirely, so most shared application state should just go into one big context that components read from with useContext wherever needed.
misconceptions.clarification: Bundling many pieces of state, especially frequently changing ones, into one context value makes every consumer re-render when ANY piece changes, whichever field a given consumer reads. That can cause more re-rendering across a large tree than the prop drilling it replaced. Context suits relatively stable, widely needed values (theme, authenticated user, locale); it isn't a cost-free replacement for local state or ordinary props.

misconceptions.description: Since useContext just reads a value, calling it doesn't cause a component to re-render unless something else about that component's own props or state also changed.
misconceptions.clarification: useContext explicitly subscribes the calling component to that context. Whenever the nearest Provider above it supplies a new value (a new reference), every component subscribed via useContext re-renders because of that subscription alone, whether or not its own props or state changed.
misconceptions.fact: useContext explicitly subscribes the calling component to that context.

exercises.prompt: Clicking "Toggle theme" is supposed to affect only ThemeLabel, but the console shows UserGreeting re-rendering every time too (both components are wrapped in memo, so App's own re-render isn't the cause). Find the cause and describe a fix.
hints: value is a single object built inside App on every render. What happens to its reference when ANY state inside App changes, even state UserGreeting doesn't use?
useContext subscribes a component to the context's value AS A WHOLE. Can React know that UserGreeting only destructures user and never touches theme?

What would change if user state and theme state each lived in their own context, with their own Provider, instead of one shared object? And what must you do so each Provider's value doesn't change on every App render?
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original code bundles user and theme into one value object, rebuilt on every render of App. Toggling theme re-renders App and produces a new value object, so every consumer of AppContext re-renders, including UserGreeting, which only reads user. Splitting into two contexts fixes this, provided each value is memoized: with `useMemo(() => ({ user, setUser }), [user])`, UserContext's value changes only when user changes (setUser is stable), so toggling theme affects only ThemeContext's value, and UserGreeting, which subscribes only to UserContext, stops re-rendering. Without the `useMemo`, the inline `{ user, setUser }` object would be new on every App render and UserGreeting would still re-render.

assessments.prompt: A context's value is an object like { cartItems, cartTotal, wishlist, currentUser }, consumed via useContext by dozens of components across a large app, including a MiniCartIcon that only ever reads cartItems.length. What happens to MiniCartIcon when wishlist changes?
options: It depends on whether MiniCartIcon is wrapped in React.memo -- with React.memo, it would never re-render for any reason.

MiniCartIcon re-renders anyway, because useContext subscribes it to the context's value as a whole object; a new value reference (caused by wishlist changing) re-renders every consumer, regardless of which specific field each one reads.
Nothing -- useContext only re-renders a component when the specific field it destructures out of the value actually changes.
MiniCartIcon throws a runtime error, since it isn't supposed to be affected by a field it doesn't read.
assessments.explanation: useContext subscribes to the context's value as a single unit; React tracks whether that value's reference changed, not which fields a consumer reads. Since wishlist changing produces a new value object reference (assuming, as is typical, the value is rebuilt whenever any of its state changes), every consumer re-renders, MiniCartIcon included, even though cartItems.length is unaffected. The “MiniCartIcon throws a runtime error, since…” option is false: nothing throws; it's a performance cost, not an error. The “It depends on whether MiniCartIcon is wrapped…” option is wrong: React.memo only skips re-renders caused by a parent re-rendering with unchanged props; it doesn't block a re-render triggered by a context the component reads, since that comes from the subscription, not a prop comparison.

options: "blue" -- useContext resolves to the value from the nearest enclosing Provider above the calling component.
"light" -- createContext's own default value always takes priority whenever a component is wrapped by more than one Provider for the same context.
"dark" -- the outermost Provider in the tree always takes priority.
An error -- a given context can only be supplied by one Provider per component tree.
assessments.explanation: useContext resolves to the nearest Provider for that context above the calling component, ignoring any Provider further out. Inner sits inside Outer's <ThemeContext.Provider value="blue">, which is nested inside App's <ThemeContext.Provider value="dark">; the inner one is nearest, so Inner displays "blue". App's "dark" only reaches consumers between App's Provider and Outer's Provider, and is shadowed inside Outer's. createContext's default ("light") is used only when a consumer has no enclosing Provider at all; it never overrides an actual Provider, ruling out the “"light" -- createContext's own default value always…” option. Nesting several Providers for the same context is valid, ruling out the “An error -- a given context can…” option.
